US Elections

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......we take a look at the US elections taking place on Tuesday 3 November

Unique Selling Point:
Very topical, newsworthy event, affects the whole of South Africa

Summary:
The US elections take place on the 3rd of November and we should take note of it – because it is an incredible spectacle and because it affects us directly. One can look at it on the 1st of November, before the election and explain how American elections work, because they are so different. The electoral college system got Trump elected in 2016, although he got less actual votes than Hillary. And what is the issue with mail-in votes. One can also take a brief look at the polarizing left-right conflict and how what is taking place in the US is, is affecting us, and Africa. The US has an enormous cultural and ideological influence on South Africa, such a the BLM movement, etc. Or one can wait a week or so until the election is over and see what is going on – there will be claims of a stolen election and missive civil unrest as the US descend into madness.

Further information:
The US elections take place on the 3rd of November and we should take note of it – because it is an incredible spectacle and because it affects us directly. One can look at it on the 1st of November, before the election and explain how American elections work, because they are so different. The electoral college system got Trump elected in 2016, although he got less actual votes than Hillary. And what is the issue with mail-in votes. One can also take a brief look at the polarizing left-right conflict and how what is taking place in the US is, is affecting us, and Africa. The US has an enormous cultural and ideological influence on South Africa, such a the BLM movement, etc. Or one can wait a week or so until the election is over and see what is going on – there will be claims of a stolen election and missive civil unrest as the US descend into madness.

Potential interviewees:
Ambassador Lana Marks -- US Ambassador in South Africa
Mr Brooks Spector -- Former diplomat, now analyst
Prof John Stremlau -- former diplomat, now analyst
Anand Naidoo -- SA Journalist working for CCNTV in USA, with own political show


Further background: Economy
The 2020 US election set for 3 November could have a direct influence on South Africa’s economy, especially when considering the policy expectations of the two candidates says Dr Greg Cline, head of corporate accounts at Investec for Business.

“Global geopolitical events will be definitive in the coming months,” said Cline.

“The US elections in November is also likely to have a ripple effect on trade, which has seen a strong recovery, despite the trade war which has led to diversion of trade flows away from both China and the US and the lockdown ensued by Covid-19.”

While both candidates, Joe Biden and Donald Trump, will remain tough on trade with China – Trump, for the most part, is likely to continue focusing heavily on tariffs . As such, markets can likely expect further escalation in the trade war, should he be re-elected, said Cline.

“The Biden administration doesn’t seem to be overly critical of some of the trade deals that have been put in place concerning China,” he said.

“More importantly, the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) – a centrepiece of economic trade partnership with South Africa and US – expires in 2025.

“While $9 billion worth of trade is estimated to transact between the two countries, the Trump administration has reviewed the agreement and identified South Africa as being restrictive and as such, agreement renewal in its current form would not be guaranteed under a Trump administration.”

Despite the uncertainty, Cline said that ‘we are now in a growth economy’ and while far off from pre-Covid levels, there is a slowdown in economic deterioration but significant changes to US policy could mean inherent risks to South Africa’s economic growth and trade.

“The foreign exchange risk appears to be contained at this time,” said Cline. The Investec-expected case for USD exchange rate forecast is R16.50 to the dollar for this quarter with a breakthrough of the R16 level by the end of the year, he said.

“Considering that South Africa is a trillion rand import economy, this may provide a level of comfort to those expecting the rand to weaken considerably further. While export pricing has thus been attractive this year, the expectation is for the imports market to recover in line with the rand.”

Expect increased volatility

The supply side of the curve is well on the way to recovery, but the economic pivot relies on assistance with the demand curve.

However, Cline said that market volatility has historically increased ahead of elections given knee-jerk reactions to election outcomes.

“We are always going to be passengers to market movements and forex fluctuations on the back of international relations and the strength of the rand is a big determinant.

“While some may argue that South Africa is in a debt spiral, with the bond yield curve suggesting the potential for sovereign default at some point in the future, there is significant Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) potential that will be realised through political certainty and strong fiscal policy locally and globally.”

“To this end, the prosperity of business locally is highly dependent on the ability to trade, coupled with a stable economic outlook, and it is our responsibility as business leaders to look for the affirmation and build a vision of South Africa that is pragmatic while contemplating numerous global risks brought about by factors out of our control,” he said.

Script:


V/O:
After 18 months of fierce in-fighting, court cases, mass protests, grinding of teeth, tearing up of speeches and name calling, America is finally on the brink of selecting their Commander in Chief for the next 4 years.

And how this individual is selected, is no simple matter, says Prof John Stremlau of Wits University.
29


7
Stremlau:
Well the election system of the Unites States is complicated and particularly for South Africans who have an independent electoral commission for the entire nation and a constitution which privileges human rights – one person one vote. The US constitution is a States Rights Constitution, so you have a federation of 50 states and they all have to have a vote for the President.
V/O:
Under this system each state is assigned a certain weight according to their population. This weight is expressed in terms of electoral votes assigned to each state. For example, California with 40 million people has 55 electoral votes and New Hampshire with only 1,4 million people, has four votes.

If a candidate wins a majority in a state, they claim all the electoral votes, irrespective of actual votes cast. In total there are 538 electoral votes up for grabs.

Brooks Spector is a former Unites States Diplomat who now lives in South Africa and writes for the Daily Maverick.
25
Brooks:
If there are 538 electoral votes, that means the winner needs 270.
V/O:
So, the number of electoral votes is the determining factor. The total number of votes cast, or popular votes, do not come into play at all.
10
LINK:
This means that the person with the most votes will not necessarily win the election. Remember this is what happened in 2016 when Hilary Clinton lost to Donald Trump.
V/O:
Back then Trump was credited with 304 electoral votes, while Hillary Clinton’s tally was 227. This meant that Trump was declared the winner, although Clinton had in fact, amassed three million more popular votes than Trump.

Further, American elections can be quite colourful.
9
LINK:
Only Donald Trump and Joe Biden stand a realistic chance of winning the White House. But on Tuesday Americans can vote for at least 20 other Presidential candidates who also appear on the ballots. Like: RAPPER KANYE WEST WHO IS STANDING AS AN INDEPENDENT, or H. BROOKE PAIGE OF THE GRUMPY OLD PATRIOTS PARTY, or GARY SWING OF THE BOILING FROG PARTY
V/O:
The raging Covid-19 pandemic in the US has already had a significant effect on the election. An unprecedented number of Americans have decided to vote through absentee votes, mail in votes, or by going to polling stations and casting early votes in order to avoid the crowds on election day.
20
Brooks:
As of this date, the recording of this conversation, something like 60 million have voted by absentee or advanced balloting.
V/O:
After two explosive presidential debates, Trump’s bout with Covid, accusations of corruption against Biden’s family, and several faux pas on both sides, the most recent polls suggest Biden is several percentage points ahead of Trump. But poll numbers are not an indication that he will win.
19
Brooks:
Polls are not predictive, they are simply a description of what the opinion is at this moment, when the question was asked.
V/O:
The polls further suggest that there is an eagerness to vote. And it is also her experience that the majority of Americans indeed favour Biden, says Nadia Neophyto, a journalist living and working in New York.
13

Nadia:
There has been such an incredible buzz and build up to this election, more so than 2016. And I think a lot of people are feeling gatvol. It is such a great word. It has a sense of people being fed up. The last four years have brought so may challenges but this year in particular – the pandemic. People are so fed up with the way the President has handled it, and thatis why we are seeing people come out in greater numbers to vote in way that they have not done before.
LINK:
Part of the spectacle of a US election is the role of celebrities who with great fanfare would endorse a particular candidate.
Nadia:
Celebrity endorsement is huge it is also quite trendy to have someone like Mark Ruffalo, he plays the Hulk. He tweets and he tells you to go and vote and tells you who to vote for and who not to vote for. It is incredibly huge. We saw Jennifer Aniston earlier this week, she posted on Instagram when she went to cast her vote that voting for Khanye West’s party is not funny and him responding to that. So, I imagine that for a lot of them they feel a social responsibility right now but also because so much is at stake. It is almost like it is all hands on deck.
V/O:
Whatever the outcome of the election, it will have ramifications for South Africa – including significant economic ones.
LINK:
Thought is various mission overseas the United States has been channelling significant financial Aid to countries like South Africa.
V/O:
In fact, the US has been providing South Africa with billions of dollars to fight HIV and Aids and this has continued under Trump. However, last year the administration threatened to cut the aid, something that could very well happen during a second Trump term, especially since Trump’s language speaks volumes about his attitude towards African and third world countries.
28
Nadia:
The fact that he had said something towards us, the countries in Africa being shithole countries, I don’t know if you are going to beep that out, but um, he has just set this incredible precedent of the language and the words that he has used that you would never think that the leader of this country of the United states of America would ever say.
V/O:
Losing the Aid would be a humanitarian disaster, but South Africa’s economy could really be hurt if Trump were to cancel AGOA, the African Growth an Opportunities Act.
10
Brooks:
Congress passed, and the President therefor signed to allow several thousand products from Africa to be exported to the United States without tariffs or duties.
V/O:
This has made the US one of South Africa’s biggest trading partners.
4
Brooks:
Under Trump it would not be there for sure because his trade status is not to give anything away. It is you give, I take, you give, I take.
V/O:
If this is cancelled, it would be a severe blow to our economy. Under Biden the act will most probably remain in place. 8
LINK:
Another major difference between Joe Biden and Donald Trump is their take on climate change and that could have a direct impact on the quality of our lives here in South Africa.
V/O:
And here in Southern Africa we are especially vulnerable to changes in our climate. Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement in 2017 is an indication that he is quite sceptical about climate change. A Biden Administration is likely to take climate change more seriously.
17
Brooks:
The country as a whole will shift toward greener renewable energy. That has got to be good for us all if we breathe and if we like to live in an environment which is too hot to exist in.
V/O:
What is also interesting about this election is that the Democratic candidate is not what one would expect from a progressive and woke party. An elderly white male candidate seemed extremely unlikely, but in the end, he was the choice of the party. But perhaps there is some logic in the decision.
19
Nadia:
It is an interesting situation. I have heard the word “harm reduction” quite a lot. You are not voting for the person you would really, really want to be in office, you are just voting for somebody who will take this country out of the situation it is right now.
V/O:
This coming week we will know if the strategy has worked. Of course, many factors play a role in people’s decision to vote for either Biden or Trump, but analysts believe that the way the Covid-19 pandemic has been managed, could be the deciding factor. 17
Brooks:
Most demographics believe that Covid and its bad handling under the current administration is the single most important issue facing the country right now.
V/O:
And voters will vote for the candidate they believe would be most effective in fighting the resurging pandemic.

And in a really worrisome development this election has revealed that many Americans do not trust their election process any longer.
16
Masa:
For the first time we are hearing it from both sides, this unwillingness to accept the outcome. I mean, it is unheard of.
Stremlau:
Only 22% of the American people have confidence in the election and that lack of confidence may have been exacerbated by Donald Trump’s rhetoric. If it is a close election it could get very, very messy. That contingency does not seem to me to be likely and the polling averages suggest that Biden’s lead is comfortable enough to prevent it, but it could happen and if it did happen it would be a crisis, the likes of which Americans have not seen since the Civil war.

Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement in 2017 is an indication that he is quite sceptical about climate change. A Biden Administration is likely to take climate change more seriously. 17 Brooks: The country as a whole will shift toward greener renewable energy. That has got to be good for us all if we breathe and if we like to live in an environment which is too hot to exist in. V/O: What is also interesting about this election is that the Democratic candidate is not what one would expect from a progressive and woke party. An elderly white male candidate seemed extremely unlikely, but in the end, he was the choice of the party. But perhaps there is some logic in the decision. 19 Nadia: It is an interesting situation. I have heard the word “harm reduction” quite a lot. You are not voting for the person you would really, really want to be in office, you are just voting for somebody who will take this country out of the situation it is right now. V/O: This coming week we will know if the strategy has worked. Of course, many factors play a role in people’s decision to vote for either Biden or Trump, but analysts believe that the way the Covid-19 pandemic has been managed, could be the deciding factor. 17 Brooks: Most demographics believe that Covid and its bad handling under the current administration is the single most important issue facing the country right now. V/O: And voters will vote for the candidate they believe would be most effective in fighting the resurging pandemic. And in a really worrisome development this election has revealed that many Americans do not trust their election process any longer. 16 Masa: For the first time we are hearing it from both sides, this unwillingness to accept the outcome. I mean, it is unheard of. Stremlau: Only 22% of the American people have confidence in the election and that lack of confidence may have been exacerbated by Donald Trump’s rhetoric. If it is a close election it could get very, very messy. That contingency does not seem to me to be likely and the polling averages suggest that Biden’s lead is comfortable enough to prevent it, but it could happen and if it did happen it would be a crisis, the likes of which Americans have not seen since the Civil war.

metadata.Summary: The US elections take place on the 3rd of November and we should take note of it – because it is an incredible spectacle and because it affects us directly. One can look at it on the 1st of November, before the election and explain how American elections work, because they are so different. The electoral college system got Trump elected in 2016, although he got less actual votes than Hillary. And what is the issue with mail-in votes. One can also take a brief look at the polarizing left-right conflict and how what is taking place in the US is, is affecting us, and Africa. The US has an enormous cultural and ideological influence on South Africa, such a the BLM movement, etc. Or one can wait a week or so until the election is over and see what is going on – there will be claims of a stolen election and missive civil unrest as the US descend into madness.

One can look at it on the 1st of November, before the election and explain how American elections work, because they are so different. The electoral college system got Trump elected in 2016, although he got less actual votes than Hillary. And what is the issue with mail-in votes. One can also take a brief look at the polarizing left-right conflict and how what is taking place in the US is, is affecting us, and Africa. The US has an enormous cultural and ideological influence on South Africa, such a the BLM movement, etc. Or one can wait a week or so until the election is over and see what is going on – there will be claims of a stolen election and missive civil unrest as the US descend into madness. Potential interviewees: Ambassador Lana Marks -- US Ambassador in South Africa Mr Brooks Spector -- Former diplomat, now analyst Prof John Stremlau -- former diplomat, now analyst Anand Naidoo -- SA Journalist working for CCNTV in USA, with own political show Further background: Economy The 2020 US election set for 3 November could have a direct influence on South Africa’s economy, especially when considering the policy expectations of the two candidates says Dr Greg Cline, head of corporate accounts at Investec for Business. “Global geopolitical events will be definitive in the coming months,” said Cline. “The US elections in November is also likely to have a ripple effect on trade, which has seen a strong recovery, despite the trade war which has led to diversion of trade flows away from both China and the US and the lockdown ensued by Covid-19.” While both candidates, Joe Biden and Donald Trump, will remain tough on trade with China – Trump, for the most part, is likely to continue focusing heavily on tariffs . As such, markets can likely expect further escalation in the trade war, should he be re-elected, said Cline. “The Biden administration doesn’t seem to be overly critical of some of the trade deals that have been put in place concerning China,” he said. “More importantly, the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) – a centrepiece of economic trade partnership with South Africa and US – expires in 2025. “While $9 billion worth of trade is estimated to transact between the two countries, the Trump administration has reviewed the agreement and identified South Africa as being restrictive and as such, agreement renewal in its current form would not be guaranteed under a Trump administration.” Despite the uncertainty, Cline said that ‘we are now in a growth economy’ and while far off from pre-Covid levels, there is a slowdown in economic deterioration but significant changes to US policy could mean inherent risks to South Africa’s economic growth and trade. “The foreign exchange risk appears to be contained at this time,” said Cline. The Investec-expected case for USD exchange rate forecast is R16.50 to the dollar for this quarter with a breakthrough of the R16 level by the end of the year, he said. “Considering that South Africa is a trillion rand import economy, this may provide a level of comfort to those expecting the rand to weaken considerably further. While export pricing has thus been attractive this year, the expectation is for the imports market to recover in line with the rand.” Expect increased volatility The supply side of the curve is well on the way to recovery, but the economic pivot relies on assistance with the demand curve. However, Cline said that market volatility has historically increased ahead of elections given knee-jerk reactions to election outcomes. “We are always going to be passengers to market movements and forex fluctuations on the back of international relations and the strength of the rand is a big determinant. “While some may argue that South Africa is in a debt spiral, with the bond yield curve suggesting the potential for sovereign default at some point in the future, there is significant Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) potential that will be realised through political certainty and strong fiscal policy locally and globally.” “To this end, the prosperity of business locally is highly dependent on the ability to trade, coupled with a stable economic outlook, and it is our responsibility as business leaders to look for the affirmation and build a vision of South Africa that is pragmatic while contemplating numerous global risks brought about by factors out of our control,” he said.
